Sodium-ion batteries establish a foothold as a lithium alternative, unlocking value from supply chain diversity and cold weather performance

05 November 2026
3 minute read

Email
Share by email

Sodium-ion batteries (SIB) are entering commercial production with over 70GWh of supply agreements, signalling confidence among downstream clients, according to a new analysis from Wood Mackenzie. 
The report called 'Sodium-ion batteries: commercialisation begins, economics to follow', which covers China, the US, Germany, and India, finds that SIB is establishing itself as the most cost-effective emerging alternative to lithium-ion battery storage. The analysis shows while cell-level parity with lithium iron phosphate (LFP) amongst market leaders is expected by end of 2026, module and system level cost parity will be attained post 2030.  
"SIB wins on supply chain security, cycle life and wide thermal threshold," said Ankita Chauhan, Director, Global Supply Chain and Integrated Power & Renewables Research at Wood Mackenzie. "Geopolitical supply advantages and superior performance of SIB across temperature ranges drive near-term commercialisation”. 
Sodium carbonate vs lithium carbonate price index comparison 
 
Source: Wood Mackenzie  
China leads, manufacturing capacity ahead of demand 
According to Wood Mackenzie, BYD has 30 GWh of planned manufacturing capacity in China, while CATL is targeting at least 1 GWh of SIB shipments by end-2026. China, the US and Europe have significant offtake agreements, whereas India is in the early commercial validation stage. China's learning rate of 18–20% during the 2026-35 period is the most mature in the sector, reflecting the commercialisation ambitions of the market leaders. 
Higher upfront cost, lower lifetime cost 
SIB command higher upfront capital with global average at 229$/kWh versus 200$/kWh for LFP but deliver 21% lower total cost of ownership (TCO). The lower TCO over a 20-year project life stems from eliminating augmentation events and lowering operating expenditure. System economics remain stable across 2 to 4 hour durations, though regional supply-chain and trade barriers present near-term headwinds to deployment. However, China's export controls, India's underdeveloped supply chain, slow US gigafactory expansion, and German trade policies risk constraining near-term growth across key markets.  
Policy outpaces cost as the key market driver 
China's reimposition of a consumption tax on lithium-ion in July 2026 explicitly exempts sodium-ion through end-2028, while LFP faces a 2% levy from September 2026, rising to 4% from September 2027. In the US, ection 301 tariffs of approximately 58% on Chinese energy storage cells structurally incentivise domestic SIB production, complemented by IRA 45X manufacturing credits. In Europe, carbon-footprint disclosure requirements under the EU Battery Regulation act as a structural tailwind, while India is building local capacity through a $1.25 billion incentive scheme and duty exemptions on manufacturing equipment, Wood Mackenzie noted. 
"The 2030-2035 window is where the economics decisively shift," said Priya Shrivastava, Senior Research Analyst, Power & Renewables, Battery Storage Supply Chain at Wood Mackenzie. For projects being deployed today, LFP remains the bankable choice for 2 to 4 hour duration assets. While SIB offers manufacturers a valuable alternative, the chemistry still faces material challenges: scaling production, refining cell materials, and establishing a track record of consistent performance. The most probable outcome is a battery market served by different technologies, each optimized for distinct applications and duration profiles.
